items.title: 10-year at 5.20%: Treasuries can finally make stocks compete
items.idea: The 10y opened the week at 5.20%, the highest in 19 years. Authers' framing: the rout hurts holders of long bonds but gives investors a real alternative to equities for the first time in a generation, so equity earnings promises now face a buyer with options. Shiller's long-run view leaves little room for disappointment.
items.angle: The equity-risk-premium debate reopens from the rates side, not the earnings side. It ties to the crowded AI-led index at records.
items.tweetA: 5.20% on the 10-year and the S&P still sits at records. Either earnings grow into a 19-year-high discount rate, or the equity buyer base is about to get a lot pickier. I don't think it's the first one.
items.tweetB: Every 'TINA' trade of the last 15 years quietly died this month. Equities used to be the only place to earn a real return. At 5.2% risk-free, the burden of proof just flipped to $SPY.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Goldman TMT desk (Peter Callahan)
items.title: Record highs, record angst: breadth at dot-com lows
items.idea: Goldman's 10 Things note calls the tone 'reserved optimism with angst and fatigue'. The sentiment indicator is firmly negative while the index grinds to records. AI leadership is doing most of the lifting; CPUs are hot while obvious AI bellwethers lag; some cheap tech names are cheap because the market doubts earnings durability.
items.angle: Narrow leadership plus negative sentiment is a positioning setup, not a valuation call. The CPU-vs-GPU rotation is worth watching inside semis.
items.tweetA: Index at records. Breadth at dot-com lows. Sentiment negative. That's not a bull market, that's a handful of stocks with a very large fan club. The question is who's left to buy when they stall.
items.tweetB: Weird tell inside semis: CPUs are working while the AI bellwethers lag. Agentic workloads are CPU-heavy, and the market is starting to price it before the sell-side does. $AMD $INTC $ARM

items.title: China: 14.8% of global exports, 9.8% of imports
items.idea: In 2025 China took 14.8% of global merchandise exports but only 9.8% of imports. Export share is steady; import share is down from its 2021 peak as domestic demand trails production. Cheaper machinery helps buyers and hurts rival producers. AI lifts some Chinese profits while competition erodes others. BlackRock likes physical AI in China.
items.angle: A five-point gap in trade share is the deflation export in one number. It sets up tariff and currency friction for everyone else.
items.tweetA: China: 14.8% of world exports, 9.8% of world imports. That 5-point gap is somebody else's factory closing. Everyone debating tariffs should be looking at who absorbs it.
items.tweetB: Chinese machinery getting cheaper AND better is a much harder problem for German and Japanese capital goods than tariffs ever were. Quality is the new front. $SIE $6861

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / BlackRock Weekly Commentary
items.title: BlackRock: bond markets may have overpriced Fed hikes
items.idea: Same BlackRock note argues bond markets may have gone too far in pricing Fed hikes. This sits against a 10y at 5.20% and oil near 94, where the market is clearly debating a re-tightening.
items.angle: Contrarian read against the rate-shock narrative; interesting next to Authers' 5.20% piece.
items.tweetA: BlackRock says the curve is pricing too many Fed hikes. Fine. But with crude at $94 and the 10y at 5.2%, who is the marginal seller of duration if they're wrong?
items.tweetB: If hikes are overpriced, then 5.2% is a gift. If they're not, it's a warning. The Iran headline decides which. Rates are now an oil trade.

items.title: The Fed is betting the ranch on the K-shaped economy
items.idea: Video note (4 min). Snippet only: the Fed, perhaps unknowingly, is betting the ranch on the K-shaped economy being particularly special, hoping for a productivity prize at the bottom of the box. Full body is paywalled; only the thesis line was readable.
items.angle: K-shape as the reason policy transmits unevenly: high-income holders benefit from higher rates, the bottom feels credit tightness.
items.tweetA: Fed policy is built for an economy that no longer exists. When the top of the K holds the assets and the bottom holds the debt, higher rates are a transfer, not a brake.
items.tweetB: The Fed is implicitly betting on a productivity miracle to rescue a K-shaped economy. That's not a forecast, that's a hope with a dot plot.

items.title: SPY range-bound for 2 months; the market needs an Iran deal
items.idea: SPY has been in a tight range for two months: dips are shallow and gains get faded. Oil, rates and VIX were up Monday, pressuring the market, with a big Trump announcement pending that afternoon. Bull flag, but 'wall of worry' can't hold forever; an Iran deal would flush oil and rates and unlock the breakout.
items.angle: Practitioner read: the breakout is a single-variable bet on the Iran outcome via oil and rates.
items.tweetA: Two months of shallow dips and faded rallies. The whole tape is one binary: Iran deal or no deal. Everything else is noise around $CL and the 10-year.
items.tweetB: If a deal 'flushes oil and rates' and unlocks the breakout, the flip side is that no deal caps both. You're not long SPY here, you're long a diplomatic outcome. Size accordingly.

items.title: Crude at $94.37, +2.08% on the morning
items.idea: Futures snapshot: crude 94.37 (+2.08%), SPX futures -0.34%, Nasdaq -0.57%. Combined with Bulltard's note that oil and rates pressured the tape, energy is the swing variable.
items.angle: Oil near 94 keeps the rate-hike question alive and explains the tape.
items.tweetA: Crude +2% to $94 and equity futures red. Same story as every morning this month: the equity market is a derivative of the barrel.
items.tweetB: At $94 oil, every 'soft landing' model has an energy tax baked in that sell-side decks don't show. Watch $XLE vs $SPY on the next Iran headline.

items.title: NVDA lifts buyback authorization by $150B
items.idea: Nvidia added $150B to its buyback authorization, bringing remaining authorization to $235B, expected to run through fiscal 2028.
items.angle: Capital return at that scale competes with capex and M&A; a signal on how management views their own cash generation.
items.tweetA: $235B of buyback authorization at Nvidia. That's larger than the market cap of most of the S&P 500 members. The AI trade is now also a capital-return trade.
items.tweetB: Nvidia buying back stock while its customers borrow to build data centers. One side of that trade is funding the other. $NVDA

items.title: Potential $100B Solidigm IPO hits SK Hynix
items.idea: SK Hynix shares fell after a report of a potential $100B Solidigm IPO. Also: Bernstein reiterated IREN bull case, $100 PT, hinging on GPU clusters coming online and ARR above $4B by December.
items.angle: Memory and neocloud valuations both being marked in public markets at scale.
items.tweetA: A $100B Solidigm IPO would price enterprise NAND as an AI asset. $SKHY fell on the headline, which tells you how the market values the parent's stake.
items.tweetB: IREN's bull case is 'GPU clusters come online and ARR hits $4B by December.' That's an execution bet dressed as an analyst note. $IREN

items.title: MongoDB CEO leaves for Meta; MDB -15% pre-market
items.idea: Former MongoDB CEO Chirantan 'CJ' Desai steps down to become Meta's Chief Enterprise Platform Officer. MDB fell as much as 15% pre-market.
items.angle: Meta hiring an enterprise-platform chief is a signal about where its AI monetization goes.
items.tweetA: Meta hires a database CEO as 'Chief Enterprise Platform Officer'. Read that title carefully. $META is building an enterprise stack, and $MDB just lost 15% of its value in a morning.
items.tweetB: Key-man risk priced at -15% in pre-market. A CEO leaving for a big-tech platform job is also an admission of where the enterprise data layer is heading.

items.title: FDA approves Lilly's once-weekly basal insulin Onswik
items.idea: FDA approved Eli Lilly's Onswik for adults with type 2 diabetes, cutting annual injections by 300+ versus daily basal insulin. LLY rose as much as 3.1%.
items.angle: Adherence-driven pharma economics: weekly dosing extends the duration of the franchise.
items.tweetA: Weekly insulin cuts 300+ injections a year. Adherence, not efficacy, is the moat in chronic disease. $LLY
items.tweetB: Lilly keeps stacking approvals in metabolic disease. The next question is what payers do with insulin pricing when the injection count drops 85%.

items.title: ServiceNow cuts ~300 roles, headcount flat, mix shifts to AI
items.idea: NOW began layoffs of nearly 300 roles as part of a plan to hold total headcount flat through year-end while shifting toward AI-focused roles.
items.angle: The pattern: flat headcount, changing composition. Labor substitution shows up as mix, not totals.
items.tweetA: Headcount flat, roles swapped. That's what AI displacement looks like in the data: it never shows up in the totals. $NOW
items.tweetB: 300 layoffs at ServiceNow isn't the story. Flat total headcount is. Every software company is quietly re-mixing labor toward the models.

items.title: Red day, but profits taken into strength: META >740, CRDO 206s, CIFR 19s
items.idea: SixSigma says red overall, though 6-7 positions were green. They took profits last week (META above 740, CRDO into the 206s), exited CIFR in the 19s, and hold cash to be opportunistic.
items.angle: Practitioner positioning: selling AI strength while breadth is narrow.
items.tweetA: Trimming $META >740 and $CRDO in the 206s last week looks smart today. Cash is a position when breadth is at dot-com lows.
items.tweetB: Everyone sells into strength in theory. Very few did in the week the index made records. The ones who did have optionality now.

items.title: The pattern behind Bitcoin's breakouts
items.idea: BTC is under pressure after a decisive move above $80K; two breakouts in two months for different reasons. Rolling ETF demand still points to positive returns but inflows are fading after the breakout just as financial conditions tighten. Paid section holds the decision.
items.angle: ETF demand as a non-steady support, versus tightening financial conditions from higher yields.
items.tweetA: BTC above $80K, ETF inflows fading right after the breakout, financial conditions tightening. Breakouts that need constant inflows to hold aren't breakouts, they're rentals.
items.tweetB: Bitcoin at $80K with the 10-year at 5.2%. The cost of carry on holding a zero-yield asset just went up. Watch whether flows respond.

items.title: OpenAI wins on creating customers and distribution, not models
items.idea: a16z argues four levers exist for a durable AI business: new behavior, distribution, pricing, switching costs. Switching costs are 'basically out' (models are substitutable, even task by task); pricing is a Red Queen race. So it's behavior and distribution, where they claim OpenAI leads, via platform breadth and own chips (Jalapeno). Quote: 'the elasticity that matters is the elasticity of aggregate demand for AI.'
items.angle: A thesis with a conflict: a16z is an investor in the space. Still, the 'model layer is substitutable' claim is the useful concession.
items.tweetA: a16z concedes the model layer is 'shockingly substitutable'. If switching costs are zero and price-performance converges, the moat is distribution. That's a very different valuation framework than compute-per-dollar.
items.tweetB: Read the fine print: the thesis for OpenAI is 'consumer breadth', which is exactly what the model labs' enterprise revenue doesn't need. Somebody's investor letter is being written here.

items.title: Stable: Tether's USDT-native L1
items.idea: Stable is a purpose-built L1 for USDT settlement: StableBFT (a CometBFT-derived DPoS), EVM execution, stablecoin-denominated gas. Mainnet launched Dec 2025 with STABLE token; v1.8.0 targets throughput. Product layer: StablePay and StableEarn. Messari notes value depends on sustained transaction demand, not performance alone.
items.angle: Stablecoin issuers vertically integrating into rails: financial plumbing shift.
items.tweetA: USDT's issuer now has its own chain with gas paid in dollars. When the issuer owns the rails, third-party L1s that live off stablecoin volume become tenants. $TRX $ETH
items.tweetB: Stablecoin-denominated gas removes the fee-volatility excuse for not using crypto rails. The real test for Stable is whether merchants care about the chain at all.

items.title: The slop floods: 1 in 3 new pages has AI; ~50% of press releases
items.idea: Every third new webpage now has AI-attributable content. Press releases hit nearly 50% probability of AI text in June, doubling in a year. UK adults spend 72 min/day on news, only 8 direct to publishers; Google AI Overviews cut even the largest sites' referral traffic 22%. $240M+ has gone into shaping AI rules across four funds versus far less for AI auditing.
items.angle: Trust and verification as a scarce, monetizable layer. Publishers' traffic problem is structural.
items.tweetA: Nearly 50% of press releases are AI-written. The only documents that were supposed to be checked by lawyers. 'Source' is losing its meaning faster than anyone is pricing.
items.tweetB: 8 minutes of 72. That's how much news time UK adults give publishers directly. Distribution has been intermediated by search and AI. The traffic isn't coming back.

items.title: AI music: over half of new Deezer uploads, only 1-3% of streams
items.idea: At its June peak, over half of new music sent to Deezer was fully AI-generated, yet AI tracks are 1-3% of streams. Deezer found up to 85% of streams on AI tracks in 2025 were fraudulent, and now licenses its detection tech. UMG is suing DistroKid (~40% of new music) over distributing mass-generated AI content. Pocket FM: 93% AI content, 2.5M hours/year vs 100K two years ago; 96 titles of 770K earned >$1M each.
items.angle: Supply explosion vs demand ceiling; fraud detection becomes a business.
items.tweetA: Half the new uploads, 1-3% of the listening. AI is a supply story with no demand pull yet. Except fraud: 85% of AI-track streams were fake. That's the actual business model.
items.tweetB: Pocket FM is the counterexample: 93% AI-generated, revenue doubled once listener data fed back into production. 96 hits from 770K titles. Content economics are power laws with cheaper lottery tickets. $UMG

items.title: Jev: decision models that score options instead of generating
items.idea: TypeSafe's Jev returns typed probabilistic decisions with no text generation. Claims 70-500 ms per call vs 3-329 s for frontier LLMs, $0.042 per million input tokens with free output. Dibia's Qwen tests: scoring 7-54x faster than generating probabilities on 7B; base models near-calibrated (ECE 0.02-0.05) vs instruct (0.10-0.18); temperature scaling cut 7B instruct ECE from 0.10 to 0.03.
items.angle: Cost curve for agent hot paths: use decision models for routing/eval, LLMs for reasoning. Post-training hurts calibration.
items.tweetA: Instruct models that put 99.8% confidence on answers that are 90.6% right. Post-training makes models confident, not calibrated. Anyone running agent evals should read this.
items.tweetB: $0.042 per million input tokens, output free, 70ms latency. If routing and eval move off frontier models, the token bill for agent workflows drops by orders of magnitude. Bad for the 'tokens forever' narrative.

items.title: Great leaps in biological theory: chemiosmosis and clonal selection
items.idea: Peter Mitchell proposed chemiosmotic theory in 1961 with 'not a shred of experimental evidence' and won the Nobel in 1978 after leaving academia (Glynn Institute). Clonal selection came from Jerne, Talmage and Burnet; Burnet published in an obscure Australian journal in case he was wrong. Theory can lead evidence by decades.
items.angle: Meta-lesson on early conviction: the best theories look wrong until the instrument catches up.
items.tweetA: Mitchell had 'not a shred of experimental evidence' in 1961, and 17 years later a Nobel. The gap between the right idea and the data that proves it is where all alpha lives.
items.tweetB: Burnet published clonal selection in an obscure journal so few would see it if he was wrong. That's hedging your reputation. Every analyst does the same with footnotes.

items.title: Opus 5.5 vs GPT-6 Astra head-to-heads: Anthropic wins both
items.idea: Two head-to-heads between Opus 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra were preferred for Anthropic's outputs. Featured: Cognition's Devin plus Opus 5.5 for software tutorials. Opus demos dominate social feeds.
items.angle: Model leadership flips are now weekly; interesting next to a16z's 'models are substitutable' argument.
items.tweetA: Opus 5.5 beats GPT-6 Astra in both head-to-heads. And a16z says models are substitutable. Both can be true: leadership rotates monthly, moats don't exist.
items.tweetB: If the top model changes every month, the only durable position is the harness and distribution. That's exactly a16z's OpenAI thesis. It's also why Anthropic is pushing agents.

items.title: First 90 days at Citadel, Jane Street, Millennium, HRT
items.idea: New-grad quant packages at Jane Street or HRT are commonly reported at $400-500K in year one including sign-on; Citadel can be similar or higher. Week one is compliance and access (data entitlements can take weeks). Jane Street trains via games and OCaml; HRT gets small changes into production within weeks; Millennium runs hundreds of independent teams.
items.angle: Talent-flow signal: comp at the top of quant continues to price ahead of everything else in finance.
items.tweetA: $400-500K for a new grad on day one. Multiply by the number of firms bidding for the same 200 people. Quant comp is the cleanest read on what liquidity is worth.
items.tweetB: HRT ships to production in weeks; Jane Street trains for months first. Both are correct: one optimizes speed of learning, the other cost of a mistake.

items.title: Raise when you can, not when you must
items.idea: Jason Calacanis' recurring advice: take capital when it's cheap on reasonable terms and hold it. Cites Andreessen 2007 ('as much as you can'), Sequoia's May 2022 'Adapting to Endure' ('Capital was free. Now it's expensive'), Gurley on burn rates. Caveat: assumes discipline, not 'token-maxxing'.
items.angle: Late-cycle signal: the advice gets louder when the window feels open.
items.tweetA: 'Raise when you can' is the loudest advice at the moment it's easiest, and the 10y is at 5.2%. Founders should read the second half: spend as if the storm is already here.
items.tweetB: Token-maxxing as a startup burn category. In 2021 it was growth spend; today it's inference bills. Same failure mode, new line item.

items.title: Airbound: 1.67x payload-to-weight drone, cost per kg-km
items.idea: Airbound (21-year-old founder Naman Pushp; $37M Series A led by Greenoaks) optimizes one loss function: cost per kilogram-kilometer. Its V2 drone carries 5 kg (1.67x its own weight); Amazon's Prime Air drone is 83 lb for 5 lb (0.06x); Zipline P2 ~0.15x. Claim: if cost wins, flight takes 80% of cargo and 90% of human movement. Amazon Prime Air is operating in Richardson, Texas.
items.angle: Payload ratio as the metric that reveals which drone economics can scale to 1-cent deliveries.
items.tweetA: 0.06x for Amazon's drone, 1.67x for Airbound's. When one design carries 28 times more per pound of aircraft, the unit economics aren't a tweak, they're a different business. $AMZN
items.tweetB: Transportation sets city shape: canal to New York, container ship to Singapore, jet to Dubai. If cost per kg-km collapses in the air, the logistics real-estate around Amazon DCs is what reprices.

items.title: Marchetti's constant: commute radius stuck at ~20km since 1960
items.idea: Humans commute about 30 minutes each way; per Marchetti's Berlin study the radius grew from 2.5 km (1800) to 4.5 km (1850) to about 20 km by 1960, then stopped. Container ships are slower than in the Nixon era; planes have the same speed. Amazon went from 8 to 54 warehouses, cutting average package trips from 450 to 141 miles. Cities form where 'batch machines' meet, cars spread them out.
items.angle: Transport stagnation as a hidden constraint on urban form and housing costs.
items.tweetA: The commute radius hasn't grown since 1960. Six decades with no gain in how far people can live from work. Housing prices are partly a transportation stagnation story.
items.tweetB: Container ships are slower today than in 1970 and planes fly at the same speed. The last 50 years of 'progress' in moving atoms was optimization, not speed. Whoever breaks that gets the next Erie Canal.
